common_name: Giant Winter Spinach (Cold-Hardy Heirloom Savoy Spinach)

planting.note: Direct sow in late summer to early fall for a hardy overwintering crop, or as soon as soil can be worked in earliest spring; Giant Winter is bred to shrug off hard freezes and hold in the garden through winter cold better than most spring-sown spinach.

directions: Direct sow a half inch deep into cool, moist, fertile soil, thinning seedlings to four to six inches apart once true leaves appear. Giant Winter is an old European heirloom selected for exceptional cold hardiness and large, heavily crinkled, dark green savoy leaves that hold quality through hard freezes and short winter days far better than most spinach varieties, making it a strong choice for a Gulf Coast fall-through-winter planting. The extra-large, thick leaves are slower to bolt in cool weather and develop a sweeter, richer flavor after exposure to frost. Harvest outer leaves as needed for a cut-and-come-again crop, or cut the whole rosette once plants reach full size.

common_name: Orange Form Aechmea (Blanchetiana Bromeliad, Amber Star Bromeliad)

planting.note: Plant divisions (pups) or container-grown stock in spring once nights stay above 50°F; Aechmea blanchetiana is hardy outdoors year-round only in zone 9b-11 and needs container culture with winter protection farther north. Foliage color is most intense in bright light and fades to plain green in deep shade.

directions: Plant in fast-draining soil or a coarse bark-and-perlite mix in bright, filtered light to partial sun — full sun brings out the most intense foliage color, while deeper shade keeps leaves plain green and softer in texture. Aechmea blanchetiana is a large, clumping, terrestrial bromeliad native to the coastal restinga scrub of eastern Brazil, forming bold rosettes of broad, stiff, strap-shaped leaves that flush brilliant orange to red-orange in strong light, an effect widely used as a dramatic color accent in South Florida and Gulf Coast landscapes. In late winter to spring, a mature rosette sends up a tall, branched flower spike with small yellow flowers held above showy orange-red bracts, after which the rosette slowly declines while offsets ('pups') fill in around it to keep the clump going indefinitely. Keep the central cup filled with water where practical, water sparingly at the roots, and protect plants from temperatures below the upper 20s°F, since foliage is damaged by frost and the plant is killed outright by a hard freeze.

common_name: Heart of Flame Bromeliad (Wild Pineapple, Bromelia balansae)

planting.note: Plant offsets or container-grown stock in spring in well-drained soil; hardy outdoors year-round only in zone 9b-11, and best sited well away from foot traffic because of its formidable spines. In late winter the central leaves flush brilliant red-orange before the flower spike emerges.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in partial shade to nearly full sun, siting the clump away from paths since the narrow, arching leaves are lined edge to edge with sharp, hooked spines. Bromelia balansae is a large, terrestrial, clump-forming bromeliad native to subtropical South America (Argentina, Paraguay, southern Brazil), grown throughout the Gulf Coast and Florida as an impenetrable, low-maintenance security hedge or barrier planting as well as an ornamental accent. In late winter to early spring, the innermost leaves of a mature rosette flush an intense fiery red-orange — the 'heart of flame' that gives the plant its common name — around the same time a tall central flower spike emerges bearing clusters of small purple flowers followed by edible, tart, pineapple-relative fruit. The plant is extremely drought tolerant once established and spreads steadily by offsets into a dense, thicket-like clump; established plantings tolerate brief drops into the upper 20s°F but are killed back hard by a freeze.
